topic: The Physics of Pi: How Colliding Blocks Compute the World's Most Famous Constant
target_audience: Advanced high school students and undergraduate physics/math enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Physics of Pi: How Colliding Blocks Compute the World's Most Famous Constant
outline.target_audience: Advanced high school students and undergraduate physics/math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Setup: A Frictionless World
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: a vertical wall, a frictionless floor, and two blocks of mass 'm' and 'M'. Block 'm' starts at rest near the wall, while 'M' slides toward it from the right. We define the rules: perfectly elastic collisions where energy and momentum are conserved.
sections.example: Visualizing a tiny 1kg block sitting still while a massive 100kg block slides toward it like a slow-moving freight train.

sections.title: The Strange Phenomenon
sections.content: Observe the number of total collisions (block-block and block-wall) as we change the mass ratio. When M = m, there are 3 collisions. When M = 100m, there are 31. When M = 10,000m, there are 314. The count remarkably matches the digits of Pi.
sections.example: An animation showing a counter above the blocks ticking up: 3, 31, 314, 3141... as the mass ratio increases by powers of 100.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Laws of Conservation
sections.content: Introduce the two governing equations: 1. Conservation of Momentum (linear) and 2. Conservation of Energy (quadratic). Explain that the state of the system can be represented by the velocities (v1, v2) of the two blocks.
sections.example: Displaying the Energy Equation: (1/2)mv1² + (1/2)Mv2² = Constant. Graphically, this looks like an ellipse in a coordinate system of velocities.

sections.title: The Phase Space Transformation
sections.content: To simplify the math, we rescale the velocity of the large block to transform the energy ellipse into a perfect circle. This 'Phase Space' allows us to track the system's state as a point moving along a circular arc.
sections.example: A visual 'stretch' animation where the elongated velocity ellipse is compressed horizontally until it becomes a perfect circle, making every collision a jump along the perimeter.

sections.title: Collisions as Geometric Reflections
sections.content: Explain that every block-block collision corresponds to a reflection across a slanted line in our circle graph, and every block-wall collision is a reflection across the axis. The number of collisions is the number of 'steps' it takes for the point to travel around the circle and head back out.
sections.example: A 'bouncing beam of light' metaphor inside a circular mirror, where each bounce represents a collision between the blocks.

sections.title: The Final Connection: Why Pi?
sections.content: Derive that the angle of each 'jump' is determined by the mass ratio. As 'M' becomes much larger than 'm', the angle becomes incredibly small. The total number of jumps needed to traverse the semi-circle (Pi radians) gives us the digits of Pi.
sections.example: A zoomed-in view of the circle showing tiny arcs of length θ. Total collisions N ≈ π / θ. If M = 100^d * m, then N results in the first d+1 digits of Pi.

storyboard.title: The Setup: A Frictionless World
lecture_lines: Imagine a frictionless floor with a wall.
Small block m sits still near the wall.
Massive block M slides in from the right.
animations: Draw wall and floor (#FFFFFF), place blocks m (#00FF00) and M (#0000FF).
Animate M sliding left towards m with a yellow arrow (#FFFF00).
Pulse both blocks and display 'Elastic Collisions' (#FFA500).

storyboard.title: The Strange Phenomenon
lecture_lines: For equal masses, we count exactly three collisions.
If M is 100 times m, we get thirty-one.
These counts remarkably match the digits of Pi.
animations: Display counter 'Collisions: 0' (#FFFFFF) and mass ratio M=m (#00BFFF).
Animate 3 collisions (block-block, wall, block-block) and update counter to 3.
Change mass ratio to M=100m (#00BFFF) and show counter reaching 31.
Change mass ratio to M=10,000m (#00BFFF) and show counter reaching 314.
Highlight 314 and display \u03c0 \u2248 3.14 (#FFD700) nearby.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Laws of Conservation
lecture_lines: Conservation of energy and momentum govern every collision.
We can track the blocks using their velocities.
The energy equation forms an ellipse in velocity space.
animations: Show Momentum Eq: mv\u2081 + Mv\u2082 = C (#00FFFF) and Energy Eq: \u00bdm v\u2081\u00b2 + \u00bdM v\u2082\u00b2 = E (#FF4500).
Draw a velocity ellipse (#FFFFFF) representing the energy conservation.
Pulse a point (v\u2081, v\u2082) (#FFFF00) moving along the ellipse's edge.

storyboard.title: The Phase Space Transformation
lecture_lines: The energy ellipse makes the geometry difficult to solve.
Let's rescale the large block's velocity axis.
This transformation stretches the ellipse into a circle.
Now, every collision is a point on this circle.
The system's state moves along a circular arc.
animations: Display the scaling transformation v\u2082 \u2192 \u221a(M/m)v\u2082 (#ADFF2F).
Animate the horizontal compression of the ellipse into a circle (#FFFFFF).
Trace a point moving in steps along the circle's circumference.

storyboard.title: Collisions as Geometric Reflections
lecture_lines: A block-block collision reflects the point across a line.
A block-wall collision reflects it across the axis.
The path bounces like light inside a circular mirror.
Each collision adds one segment to the path.
We simply count these geometric reflections.
animations: Draw a circle with a slanted 'collision line' (#FF69B4).
Reflect a point across the slanted line (block-block collision).
Draw a horizontal 'wall line' (#1E90FF) and reflect the point across it.
Show a sequence of reflections bouncing between these two lines.
Zoom out to show the point traversing the circle in steps.

storyboard.title: The Final Connection: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: The mass ratio determines each reflection's small angle.
As M grows, the angle theta becomes tiny.
Total collisions equal Pi radians divided by theta.
For powers of 100, we recover Pi's digits.
Physics has just computed Pi through simple collisions.
animations: Highlight a small arc on the circle with angle \u03b8 (#FF8C00).
Display \u03b8 \u2248 \u221a(m/M) (#FFFFFF) as the mass ratio increases.
Show the full semi-circle as a path of length \u03c0 (#FFD700).
Divide \u03c0 by \u03b8 to show the number of steps N.
Reveal the final digits of \u03c0 from the collision count.
